passages.t: Two advisers, and the LORD's purpose
passages.happening:
Ahithophel gives Absalom his advice: “Let me choose twelve thousand men and set out tonight in pursuit of David. I will attack him while he is weak and weary; I will throw him into a panic, and all the people with him will flee; I will strike down only the king and bring all the people back to you as a bride returning to her husband” (verses 1-3). The plan seems good to Absalom and the elders.

But Absalom calls for Hushai too. Hushai says, “This time the advice of Ahithophel is not sound” (verse 7). David and his men are fierce, he says, ‘as fierce as a wild bear robbed of her cubs’ (verse 8), and David will be hiding somewhere, not sleeping with the troops. If Absalom's men suffer a first loss, panic will spread. Better to gather all Israel from Dan to Beersheba, as many as the sand on the seashore, with Absalom leading them himself, and fall on David like dew on the ground (verses 8-13).

Absalom and all the men of Israel choose Hushai's way: “The advice of Hushai the Archite is better than that of Ahithophel” (verse 14). And the narrator adds, ‘For the LORD had purposed to thwart the good counsel of Ahithophel in order to bring disaster on Absalom’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
This is the hinge of the revolt. On the Mount of Olives David prayed that God would turn Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness, and sent Hushai back. Here the prayer is answered, through the man David sent.

Counsel in an ancient court was a formal affair, and a senior adviser's word could decide a war. Ahithophel's plan is sound strategy: strike at once while the enemy is weary and scattered, kill the leader, spare the people. It would probably have ended David's life.

Hushai's answer is long and full of pictures: a bear robbed of her cubs, the heart of a lion melting, an army like the sand of the sea, a city dragged into a valley with ropes. It plays on Absalom's fear and flatters him with the picture of himself at the head of all Israel. And it buys David time, which is what he needs most.

Then the narrator steps in with one of the clearest comments in the book. The people choose freely, and yet the LORD had purposed to defeat the good counsel. It is one of only a few places in the long story of David's family where the narrator says outright what God is doing. God works through human decisions, not around them.
passages.later: Proverbs states the same truth: “There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel that can prevail against the LORD” (Proverbs 21:30). And a psalm sings it of whole nations: “The LORD frustrates the plans of the nations; He thwarts the devices of the peoples” (Psalm 33:10).
passages.asks: Hushai won the argument by flattering Absalom's pride. Ask where you are most open to advice that flatters you. And ask whether you believe that God can work through the ordinary decisions of the people around you.

passages.t: A warning in the night, and Ahithophel's end
passages.happening:
Hushai tells the priests Zadok and Abiathar what both men advised, and urges them to send word to David not to spend the night at the fords of the wilderness, but to cross over at once (verses 15-16).

The priests' sons, Jonathan and Ahimaaz, are waiting at En-rogel, where a servant girl brings them news. A young man sees them and tells Absalom, so they hurry to a house in Bahurim and climb down into a well in the courtyard. The man's wife spreads a cover over the mouth of the well and scatters grain on it. When Absalom's servants come asking, she tells them the two have crossed the brook. The searchers find nothing and go back to Jerusalem (verses 17-20).

The young men climb out and bring David the warning. ‘So David and all the people with him got up and crossed the Jordan. By daybreak, there was no one left who had not crossed the Jordan’ (verse 22).

When Ahithophel sees that his advice has not been followed, he saddles his donkey and goes home to his town. He puts his affairs in order and takes his own life, and he is buried in his father's tomb (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The second half of the chapter moves fast: messages, a narrow escape, a crossing by night. Wells and cisterns were common in courtyards, since households depended on stored rainwater, and grain spread out to dry on a cloth was ordinary work that would draw no attention. A woman's quick thinking saves the king's messengers, as Rahab's once saved Israel's spies.

The verb to cross runs through the chapter. David's escape depends on getting over the Jordan before Absalom's army can reach him, and by daybreak no one is left behind.

Ahithophel's end is told in a single sentence. He saw that his counsel had been rejected, and he probably foresaw that Absalom would fail, and that he, as a leading traitor, would face death.
passages.later: Rahab, too, hid the men who carried Israel's hopes: ‘But Rahab had taken them up to the roof and hidden them among the stalks of flax that she had laid out there’ (Joshua 2:6).
passages.hard:
How should a reader think about Ahithophel's death?

The text reports it briefly and without comment, and these notes do not dwell on it. The narrator neither praises nor condemns the act. The Bible records a few such deaths, among them Saul's, Ahithophel's, Zimri's and Judas's, and each is told as the tragic end of a life that had gone badly wrong. The Bible never presents taking one's own life as a good or honorable way out.

Scripture insists that human life belongs to God and that no one is beyond his mercy. Ahithophel's story shows the despair that can follow ruined plans and wounded pride. The Bible's story does not end in despair, and help is there for anyone in that kind of darkness.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: A woman with a cover and a handful of grain saved two lives. Ask what small, ordinary act of courage might be yours to do this week. And if your plans have fallen apart, ask who you could tell the truth to before the night ends.

passages.happening:
David comes to Mahanaim, and Absalom crosses the Jordan with all the men of Israel. Absalom has made Amasa commander in place of Joab. Amasa is a cousin of Joab, the son of Abigail, the sister of Joab's mother Zeruiah (verses 24-25). Absalom's army camps in the land of Gilead.

At Mahanaim David is met by Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Machir son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite. They bring beds, basins and pottery, wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans and lentils, honey, curds, sheep and cheese, for David and his people. For they said, “The people have become hungry, exhausted, and thirsty in the wilderness” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Mahanaim lay east of the Jordan in Gilead. It had been Ish-bosheth's capital after Saul's death, and it was a fortified town where David could regroup. Its name recalls Jacob, who met angels there.

The men who come with supplies are from different peoples. Shobi is from the Ammonite capital, probably a brother of Hanun, whom David had fought, and perhaps now ruling there under David. Machir had once sheltered Jonathan's lame son, Mephibosheth. Barzillai is a wealthy man of Gilead who will appear again. Kindness David showed years before is being repaid, and old enemies are now friends.

Their gifts are lavish hospitality to a king in exile, and they answer exactly what the people lack. The chapter that began with a plan to strike David while he was weary ends with weary people fed.

Amasa, Absalom's commander, was related to both David and Joab. Chronicles says that Abigail and Zeruiah were David's sisters, so Amasa and Joab were cousins and David's nephews. The note here that Abigail was the daughter of Nahash is a puzzle. Amasa's father is called an Israelite in the Hebrew of Samuel and an Ishmaelite in Chronicles, and the BSB follows Chronicles.
passages.later:
Mahanaim was named by Jacob when he met the angels of God there: “This is the camp of God” (Genesis 32:2).

Chronicles gives Amasa's family: ‘Their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail’ (1 Chronicles 2:16), and ‘Abigail was the mother of Amasa’ (1 Chronicles 2:17).
passages.asks: Friends from unexpected places fed David's people when they were worn out. Ask who has provided for you in a hard season, perhaps someone you once thought an enemy. And ask whom you could feed, in whatever way, while they are still in the wilderness.
